newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egyptian discount cut follows general rate fall.
newsitem.headline: Egyptian discount cut follows general rate fall.

text.p: The Central Bank of Egypt cut its discount rate with effect from Thursday to 13.25 percent from 13.5 percent, catching up with a general decline in interest rates. It was the first cut in the rate since November 23, 1995, when it fell half a percentage point.
Bankers say they never borrow at the discount rate, which is merely indicative of the Central Bank's intentions about interest rates in general.
It is also used as the benchmark for bonds issued by Arab Land Bank, which pays the discount rate less 1.5 percent.
The reduction is in line with a gradual decline in treasury bill rates, which since November 1995 have fallen to an average of 10.178 percent from about 10.5 percent on 91-day bills.
After a long period of stability at around 10.25 percent, rates suddenly began to slip again this month, possibly because of an influx of foreign funds into the market, bankers said.
"There's a lot of foreign interest and demand. Some banks have been bidding for 80 or 100 million pounds ($23 million to $29 million) at a time," one banker said.
Most of the T-bill auctions are for a total of between 500 and 900 million pounds.
"Foreign money is coming in and it looks like the Central Bank is encouraging it. That may be why they have offering the repos -- to show this is a sophisticated market," said another.

The Central Bank has offered a series of 500 million repos on treasury bills but private-sector banks have avoided them. The repos have tax disadvantages and the bankers say they usually have enough liquidity without them.

The bankers said they doubted treasury-bills rates would fall below the 10-percent mark in the short term, if only because the authorities want to support the Egyptian pound by keeping the rate differential between the dollar and the pound.
The pound has been more or less stable against the dollar since 1991, despite the big difference in inflation rates.
"Half a percentage point on interest rates wouldn't hit the pound and I don't see them going below 10 percent," said one.
"I don't see it below 10 percent, at least until the second half of 1997. If you are talking liquidity it should go down, but if you are talking politics, it won't happen," said another.
The government says allowing the pound to fall would damage confidence in the Egyptian economy. Hot money would run away and new investors would hesitate to move in, officials say.
